title: Isaac and Ishmael at One Grave
hookLine: mourners shovel earth into the grave themselves
carry: filling the grave is the kindness of truth

lines: ISAAC AND ISHMAEL AT ONE GRAVE.
cards: "And Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him." That's how Genesis, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, closes the story of Abraham.
Two brothers who grew up apart, one sent away into the wilderness as a boy, stand at the same grave. The text doesn't say they made peace. It says they buried their father.
Once the prayers are said, the shovel doesn't stay with the cemetery workers. The daughter picks it up. Then the brother.
Then the old friend from work. Earth lands on a plain wooden lid, slow and heavy and hard to watch. The tradition calls it a kindness.

teach.b: First, the sons at the grave. Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham. A generation later, Genesis says the same of Isaac: his sons Esau and Jacob bury him, two more brothers with a hard history.
Whatever lay between them, the burial was theirs to do. Second, the name.
Earlier this week you met Rashi's phrase for care of the dead: chesed shel emet, the kindness of truth, a kindness the one who receives it can never repay.
Filling the grave is its last act, and the tradition gives it to the people who loved the person, not only to strangers. It makes the death real. Nobody leaves the cemetery thinking it was a dream.
Third, the small customs. In some communities the first scoops are taken with the back of the blade, so it doesn't look like ordinary digging. And nobody hands the shovel over.
You push it back into the mound and step away, and the next person picks it up on their own.
Some explain the back of the shovel as reluctance, and putting it down as not handing grief from one person to the next.

teach.h: NO ONE LEFT TO THANK YOU.
teach.b: Communities give different reasons, and keep the custom anyway.
Fourth, the circle. Friends and neighbors take a turn too, because the work is shared. The person in the grave will never know who lifted the earth.
No one is left to say thank you, and the shovel goes round anyway.

how: At a Jewish burial, after the prayers, mourners and friends take turns placing earth into the grave themselves; in some communities the shovel is put back into the earth rather than handed from person to person.

o: shoveling earth into the grave for someone you loved
the last gift a person leaves in their will
the final words of praise in a eulogy

games.q: you've finished your turn with the shovel at the graveside. the next mourner is waiting. what does custom in some communities say to do?
o: hand the shovel straight to them.
push it back into the earth and step away.
keep going until the grave is full.
games.why: you put it down, and they pick it up on their own. some explain it as not passing grief from hand to hand.

practice: Bring to mind a kindness you've been putting off, not because it's big but because it's hard: a call to someone who is ill, an awkward visit.
Picture picking it up the way a mourner takes the shovel, once, with both hands, without waiting to be handed it; if you pray, hold that person in your prayer.
And if the grief you're carrying is your own and it feels like too much, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: The last kindness. Chesed shel emet, the kindness of truth: care for the dead, who can never repay it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the kindness of truth, a name for care for the dead.
